Neonatal Psittacosaurus lujiatunensis weighed approximately 250 grams [Wwb = approximately 250 grams], a value derived from the exceptional juvenile specimens preserved in the Yixian Formation. The ontogenetic series available for this ceratopsian dinosaur indicates that hatchlings emerged from relatively large, parchment-shelled eggs with a well-developed yolk sac, and their initial body mass was substantial compared to many contemporaneous ornithischians. The yolk-dependent larvae absorbed their endogenous nutrients rapidly, fueling a period of accelerated growth that continued through the early juvenile stages. The species attained its ultimate wet weight of 38,400 grams [Wwi = 38,400 grams] by early adulthood, a figure calculated from the largest known adult skeletal remains and supported by growth-ring analyses. This asymptotic mass places Psittacosaurus lujiatunensis among the smaller-bodied members of the Ceratopsia, reflecting its basal position within the clade. The transition from a lecithotrophic hatchling to a fully grown, reproductively active adult involved a remarkable increase in body mass, suggesting sustained high feeding rates throughout the growth period.

Under the paleoclimatic conditions inferred for the Early Cretaceous Jehol Biota, where mean annual temperatures likely reached approximately 37 °C [T = 37 °C], the maximum reproductive rate for Psittacosaurus lujiatunensis has been estimated at approximately 0.093 clutches per day [F_R_i = approximately 0.093 clutches per day], though this figure probably reflects the upper physiological ceiling rather than a typical field rate. Given the constraints of egg production and nesting behavior observed in related ornithischians, a female may have produced between 12 and 15 clutches annually during the breeding season. The brooding posture documented in several exceptionally preserved fossils confirms that adults incubated the clutches directly, maintaining the elevated egg temperatures necessary for successful embryogenesis at around 37 °C. This reptilian reproductive strategy, coupled with the relatively small clutch sizes inferred from pelvic dimensions, suggests a life history in which parental investment was concentrated on a moderate number of well-provisioned offspring each year.

Sexual maturity in Psittacosaurus lujiatunensis was achieved approximately 9 years after hatching [tp = approximately 9 years after hatching], a developmental milestone inferred from the pronounced changes in bone histology and external morphology visible across the growth series at a temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C]. The onset of gonadal activation, marked by the closure of certain neurocentral sutures and the development of species-typical integumentary structures, occurred at an age that aligns with the prolonged maturation periods seen in many extant reptiles of comparable adult body mass. The juvenile individuals, which retained a more gracile build and lacked the fully developed rostral and jugal horn-like processes, entered the subadult phase gradually, with the transition to reproductive maturity spanning several growing seasons. The time since birth at puberty appears to have been relatively invariant across the known specimens, suggesting a canalized developmental program despite the seasonally fluctuating resources of the lacustrine environment. This delayed maturation likely allowed sufficient time for the accumulation of skeletal reserves necessary to support the energetic demands of reproduction.

Taxonomic comparisons within the Ornithischia reveal that the lifespan of Psittacosaurus lujiatunensis extended to approximately 12 years [am = approximately 12 years] under the thermal conditions typical of the Jehol Biota at 37 °C at a temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C]. Longevity was estimated through growth-line counts in the fibulae and tibiae of the largest adult individuals, supplemented by body-size frequency distributions across the mortality assemblages. This maximum documented lifespan positions Psittacosaurus closer to the slower end of the dinosaurian spectrum, comparable to certain medium-sized theropods rather than to the extremely rapid life histories of small-bodied ornithopods. The physiological death of senescent individuals likely followed a period of reproductive decline, with the oldest adults exhibiting diminished bone density and reduced annual growth increments. The age-related changes in limb bone histology further suggest that somatic senescence was gradual, consistent with a lifestyle involving limited predation pressure on fully grown adults.

Histological examination of Psittacosaurus lujiatunensis growth series reveals that the femur and tibia exhibit lines of arrested growth which have been used to estimate individual age at death, providing a direct window into the species' life history. The spacing between successive growth marks narrows considerably after the period of sexual maturation, a pattern observed in extant reptiles where growth slows following the onset of reproductive investment. The annual cycles of bone deposition reflect seasonal variations in food availability within the Jehol Biota, where monsoon-driven rainfall alternated with drier intervals. Understanding these environmental fluctuations is critical for interpreting the physiological constraints that shaped the species' developmental trajectory and reproductive scheduling.
